intro: Piccolo, contrabassoon and three trombones join the orchestra for the C-major finale of Beethoven’s Fifth Symphony. After their entrance, the quiet C-minor music of the scherzo returns once more before the close of the movement.

sections.label: A · C major with three trombones
sections.mNote: A rising triad leads to G major.

sections.label: A · C-major opening theme, exposition repeat
sections.mNote: The exposition is played a second time.

sections.label: Dev · Running figures pass through the orchestra
sections.mNote: The bass descends by semitones in the second ending.

sections.label: B · Scherzo returns, quiet, C minor
sections.mNote: C minor, triple metre, detached string replies

sections.label: A′ · Opening theme returns in C major
sections.mNote: Piccolo, contrabassoon and trombones play the opening theme again.

sections.label: Coda · Lead-in to the Presto
sections.mNote: Quiet wind phrases grow into the repeated final chords

cues.title: Finale opening, trombones enter
cues.text: The opening climbs a triad, C–E–G. Three trombones give the chords new breadth, and piccolo and contrabassoon extend the orchestra at both ends. Beethoven held these players back until the finale.
cues.evidence: Beethoven, Werke, Serie 1 No. 5, Breitkopf & Härtel, printed p. 52, finale opening and added parts. Instrumentation discussed at https://www.esm.rochester.edu/beethoven/symphony-no-5/.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Second group in G major
cues.text: The second group is in G major. Strings and winds divide the phrases between them, and short repeated-note figures keep them moving.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed pp. 59–61, G-major second group, repeated-note figures and divided wind/string writing.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Letter to Count Oppersdorff, 1808
cues.text: In March 1808 Beethoven wrote to Count Oppersdorff about the three trombones and piccolo in the finale. He promised that it “will make more noise than 6 kettledrums and better noise at that”.
cues.evidence: Beethoven to Count Franz von Oppersdorff, March 1808; Thayer, Life of Beethoven, vol. 1, p. 433, quoted by Eastman School of Music: https://www.esm.rochester.edu/beethoven/symphony-no-5/.

cues.title: Repeat of the exposition
cues.text: The exposition repeats, returning to the opening march in C major with full brass. The music moves to G major again before Beethoven develops the themes further.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed p. 63, first ending and repeat sign returning to the C-major opening on p. 52.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Benefit concert, 22 December 1808
cues.text: Reichardt reported that Beethoven met great resistance in staging his benefit concert on 22 December 1808. The singers and orchestra were drawn from many groups, and the long, difficult programme could not be rehearsed in full. Four hours of music were played.
cues.evidence: Johann Friedrich Reichardt, Vertraute Briefe geschrieben auf einer Reise nach Wien (Amsterdam, 1810), vol. 1, letter of Vienna, 25 December 1808, pp. 255–56. Translation ours. https://archive.org/details/10623218bsb

cues.title: Second-time bar and development
cues.text: The repeated exposition now takes its second ending. The low strings and contrabassoon move down by semitones under held wind chords. Running figures pass through the strings and then the woodwind.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed pp. 63–65: second ending, chromatic bass and development figures passed through strings and woodwind.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Reichardt at the première, 1808
cues.text: The composer Johann Friedrich Reichardt watched the première from Prince Lobkowitz’s box. “There we sat, in the most bitter cold, from half past six until half past ten,” he wrote, and concluded that one may easily have too much of a good thing.
cues.evidence: Johann Friedrich Reichardt, Vertraute Briefe geschrieben auf einer Reise nach Wien (Amsterdam, 1810), vol. 1, letter of Vienna, 25 December 1808, pp. 254–55: “in der bittersten Kälte von halb 7 bis halb elf”, and that one can easily have too much of the good, and still more of the powerful. Translation ours. https://archive.org/details/10623218bsb

cues.title: Return of the scherzo
cues.text: In the C-major finale, C minor and the scherzo’s three-beat bars return. Quiet string notes leave gaps for entries from bassoon and clarinet. The trombones fall silent.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed pp. 72–75: Tempo I, 3/4 and recalled scherzo, with reduced strings and wind replies. Eastman confirms the C-minor return.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Recapitulation in C
cues.text: The quiet bridge passage builds in a crescendo, and the opening tune of the finale returns in C, with piccolo, contrabassoon and trombones. The later melodies of the recapitulation are also in C.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed pp. 75–76, crescendo and Allegro recapitulation. The second group’s return in C is discussed at https://www.esm.rochester.edu/beethoven/symphony-no-5/.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Hoffmann’s review, 1810
cues.text: E. T. A. Hoffmann reviewed the Fifth in 1810 for the Allgemeine musikalische Zeitung and called it “one of the most important works of the time”. He revised the essay in 1813 for his collection Kreisleriana.
cues.evidence: Hoffmann’s review “Beethoven’s Instrumental Music” (1810; revised 1813): Eastman School of Music, https://www.esm.rochester.edu/beethoven/symphony-no-5/; also https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._5_(Beethoven), Reception.

cues.title: Extended coda
cues.text: The coda is in two parts and gives the familiar figures another long stretch of music. Quiet wind phrases are taken up by more players, then the tempo increases through Sempre più allegro to Presto.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed pp. 86–100, coda, wind exchanges and later tempo markings; Eastman’s formal account identifies the extended two-part coda.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Letter to Franz Wegeler, 1801
cues.text: In November 1801 Beethoven wrote to his friend Franz Wegeler that he would “seize fate by the throat”, and that it should certainly never wholly overcome him. His hearing had already begun to fail.
cues.evidence: Beethoven to Franz Wegeler, 16 November, letter XXXVIII in Beethoven’s Letters, ed. A. C. Kalischer, trans. J. S. Shedlock (London: Dent, 1909), p. 35: “I will seize fate by the throat; it shall certainly never wholly overcome me.” Kalischer prints the date as “November 16 [1801 ?]”; 1801 is the usual dating. https://archive.org/details/beethovensletter01beet

cues.title: Final cadence in C major
cues.text: The orchestra plays chord after chord of C major, with rests between the attacks. Beethoven extends the final cadence well past its expected length. All the players end in unison on C.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed pp. 96–100, repeated C-major cadential gestures and final unison C. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/0/0c/IMSLP52624-PMLP01586-Beethoven_Werke_Breitkopf_Serie_1_No_5_Op_67.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Exposition repeat from G to C
transitions.from: A · C major with three trombones
transitions.to: A · C-major opening theme, exposition repeat
transitions.how: The exposition closes with G-major chords and a brief rest. The repeat brings back the opening C-major triad, C–E–G, above C in the bass. Trombones reinforce the wind and string chords, and the piccolo rises above them. The Allegro tempo continues.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed p. 63, first ending and repeat to p. 52.

transitions.title: The second ending lowers the bass
transitions.from: A · C-major opening theme, exposition repeat
transitions.to: Dev · Running figures pass through the orchestra
transitions.how: The second ending continues the G-major closing music. The bass then moves down from G through F♯ to F beneath held wind chords, and the strings play running figures that pass between parts. The Allegro continues; the figures pass to the woodwind and the harmony moves away from G.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed pp. 63–65: second ending, G–F♯–F bass and subsequent woodwind entries.

transitions.title: Return of the scherzo music
transitions.from: Dev · Running figures pass through the orchestra
transitions.to: B · Scherzo returns, quiet, C minor
transitions.how: The full orchestra holds G, the dominant of C, before Tempo I changes the metre to 3/4. The C-minor scherzo music returns in pianissimo strings. The bass plays short notes separated by rests, and bassoon and clarinet reply above. Piccolo, contrabassoon and trombones stop playing.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed pp. 72–75: held G before Tempo I, 3/4, reduced scoring and recalled scherzo.

transitions.title: Crescendo into the C-major Allegro
transitions.from: B · Scherzo returns, quiet, C minor
transitions.to: A′ · Opening theme returns in C major
transitions.how: The quiet wind phrases and repeated viola chords build through a crescendo. The strings play arco again, and the timpani enter. At the Allegro, in common time, the opening C-major tune returns over C in the bass, with piccolo, contrabassoon and all three trombones playing again.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed pp. 75–76: crescendo, arco, timpani entry and C-major Allegro.

transitions.title: Into the coda in C major
transitions.from: A′ · Opening theme returns in C major
transitions.how: The C-major closing music continues into running string figures and forceful wind chords. Cello and double bass carry the figures down into the bottom of the orchestra. The tempo stays at Allegro. Later, quiet bassoon and horn phrases begin another build towards the faster ending of the coda.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed pp. 86–90, opening stretch of the coda, running strings and subsequent quiet bassoon and horn entries.

source.title: Beethoven, Symphony No. 5, IV, Breitkopf & Härtel full score, plate B.5
source.locator: Printed pp. 52–100, finale; the recalled scherzo occupies pp. 72–75.

timeline.note: Piccolo, contrabassoon and three trombones join the C-major opening.
Strings and woodwind exchange the lighter phrases of the G-major second group.
Full wind and brass chords reinforce the strings at the exposition’s close.
The repeat brings back the C-major march with its three trombones.
The second group’s wind and string exchanges return in G major.
The closing chords return; the second ending sends the bass down by semitones.
Running figures pass through the strings and into the woodwind.
Wind and brass play chords above the moving strings.
Pianissimo string notes begin the scherzo recollection; the trombones are silent.
Oboe, clarinet and horn phrases sound above the strings. Flutes, bassoons and timpani join the approach to C major.
The full orchestra restores the C-major opening, with piccolo above and contrabassoon below.
The second group’s lighter wind and string phrases return in C major.
Full orchestral chords alternate with quiet replies from the wind as the coda speeds up.
The whole orchestra repeats the closing C-major chords and ends on a final C.

composer.epithet: Composer known for a symphony built from a four-note motif and for the string quartets of his last years.
facts: Neefe in Bonn; Haydn, Albrechtsberger and Salieri in Vienna
Bonn until 1792; Vienna and its surrounding villages for the rest of his life
Nine symphonies · five numbered piano concertos · 32 numbered piano sonatas · 16 string quartets · Fidelio
Described his hearing loss in 1801; used conversation books from 1818

quote.text: I live only in my notes.
quote.source: Beethoven to Franz Gerhard Wegeler, Vienna, 29 June 1801; our translation

composer.background:
In March 1778 Johann van Beethoven advertised a concert in Cologne by his six-year-old son. Ludwig was seven. His father, a singer in the electoral chapel at Bonn, hoped to launch another child prodigy; his grandfather, also Ludwig, had risen from singer to Kapellmeister in the same establishment. The boy was baptised on 17 December 1770, probably the day after his birth. By his teens he was playing the organ for services and the viola in the court orchestra, where he learned operas as a member of the string section.

Christian Gottlob Neefe put Bach’s Well-Tempered Clavier before him and helped him into paid employment. The Breuning household supplied books, friendship and a refuge from Johann’s drinking. After his mother died in 1787, Beethoven increasingly supported his younger brothers. In November 1792 the elector sent him to Vienna to study with Haydn. He was expected to return. French troops occupied Bonn in 1794, and the court that paid him ceased to exist.
